metadata.note: ai-explainer / claude-hai. AI Debt Tracker WEEK 2. ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, answered), B09 (verdict artifact), B10 (handoff) and B11 (outro) only — every body beat illustrates its concept as a native animated Remotion scene (REBUILD LAW). The three source PNGs and their SVG sources are REFERENCE in pantry/, never slotted as media. The script's seven sections are split into eight body beats (1:13 splits into B03 the bugs and B04 calibrated-vs-measured) and the closing on-camera section becomes a limits beat; the split is logged in BUILD-LOG.md. FOUR THINGS NOT TO GET WRONG: the agent is NOT built, only its judge; 10 of 10 is a calibration and 2 of 3 is the measurement; 90.7% is flattering and hides a zero; and 30 of 32 is the searchable denominator, not 30 of 36. VERTICAL CUT: every beat re-renders from a <pattern>916 portrait composition — a re-layout, never a crop. The narration mp3s are copied from the 16:9 reel, not regenerated, so the two masters are the same edit.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about building the answer key and the grader for my A I debt tracker, and measuring the do nothing baseline it has to beat. This is week two of the A I Debt Tracker. The agent still is not written. What this week built is the thing that will judge it, and the floor it has to clear.

shot.visual_intent: COLD OPEN LAW: the ask is the week itself — build the judge before the thing being judged. Lands ANSWERED.

props.segment: Building the Answer Key, Grader and Baseline
props.command: Before the agent exists, build what will grade it: an answer key from the real reports, a grader with a stated matching rule, and the score a do-nothing baseline already gets. Then check the grader against printed tables.
output: 1,093 reports, 100 companies, 9,653 bonds in the answer key
the grader disagreed with 2 of 10 printed tables — every disagreement was a bug in mine
and the do-nothing baseline caught 0 of 36 new bonds

beats.narration_text: The tracker is graded against each company's next quarterly report, so first that answer had to be written down. I built it for a hundred companies — twenty five A I companies and seventy five others — from one thousand and ninety three reports since January twenty twenty four. That's nine thousand six hundred and fifty three bonds. Most of those reports list debt bond by bond; some only by deal.

shot.visual_intent: ONE bar the width of the whole answer key, partitioned — not three bars, which would invite 900 to be compared with 41. The segments ARE the 1,093 counted above them.

show.at: on each of the three numbers

show.event: One full-width bar splits into the three grading levels.

props.subtitle: Every quarterly and annual report, Jan 2024 – Sep 2026, read from SEC filings
props.levelsLabel: How much detail each report gives
props.unseenNote: The agent is not written. This week built the answer key, the grader and the baseline it will be scored against.  (not in figdata.json — from narration_script.md and the project documents)

beats.narration_text: The grader scores a debt list three ways. Bond by bond, the currency, interest rate and due year must agree, and the amount must be within one percent. And each true bond can be claimed by only one answer. Then deal by deal, and then totals. Every score comes with a confidence range, so a small difference is never oversold.

shot.visual_intent: The pairing constraint is the part a viewer would never guess, so it gets its own block rather than a clause in a footnote. SHOW the rule, do not summarise it.

show.event: Three mode cards land, coarsest last.
The four field chips land, then the pairing rule.

props.sparkLine: A score is only as honest as its rule.
props.title: Three ways to score a debt list
props.subtitle: The agent is not written yet. This is what will judge it.

modes.note: every instrument matched on four fields
grouped issuances, where that is all a report gives
one figure, for reports that give nothing finer

props.fieldsLabel: a bond matches only if all four agree
props.pairing: Each true bond can be claimed by at most one answer.
props.intervalNote: Every score carries a 95% bootstrap interval, so a small difference between two runs is never read as an improvement.

beats.narration_text: But who checks the checker? I compared the answer key with the debt tables printed in ten real reports. The first pass agreed on only eight. Every disagreement was my bug, not theirs. Oracle's repaid notes were still counted as owed. Broadcom's debt from buying V M ware had been dropped entirely. Two bonds in one entry, due dates read as issue dates, and a currency never stated.

shot.visual_intent: The honest centre of the reel. Five concrete defects, each attributed to the report that found it — not a sentence saying mistakes were made.

show.event: Five numbered rows land, each naming the company that exposed it.
The verdict lands beneath them, in the accent.

props.sparkLine: Every disagreement was my bug, not theirs.
props.eyebrow: AI DEBT TRACKER · CHECKING THE CHECKER
props.title: What the printed tables caught
props.subtitle: The answer key against the debt tables printed in 10 real 10-Qs and 10-Ks — first pass agreed on 8

bugs.bug: Due dates read as issue dates

props.verdict: were bugs in my grader, not errors in the reports.
props.source: SOURCE: AI Debt Tracker docs/handcheck.md, manifests/handcheck/ · figdata.json

beats.narration_text: After fixing all five, ten of ten. But those ten reports are what found the fixes, so ten of ten is a calibration, not a score. For the honest check I graded three untouched reports, once. Two of three agree. The one miss is that company's own data entry errors, saved for next week rather than tuned away.

shot.visual_intent: The dashed rule IS the argument: above it, reports read while the bugs were being fixed; below it, reports picked first and graded once.

show.event: The two calibration bars fill.
A dashed rule draws across, and the held-out bar lands below it.

props.sparkLine: Ten of ten is a calibration. Two of three is the score.
props.eyebrow: AI DEBT TRACKER · CALIBRATED vs MEASURED
props.title: Which of these two numbers is evidence
props.calibratedLabel: the 10 reports that FOUND the fixes
props.measuredLabel: the 3 picked first and graded once
props.missNote: The one miss is a company's own tagging errors, recorded for next week rather than tuned away. Three reports is a small check and is said as one — it is the only number here that was not read while the bugs were being fixed.
props.source: SOURCE: AI Debt Tracker docs/handcheck.md, DESIGN.md P30–P37 · figdata.json

beats.narration_text: Then the floor. The simplest possible tracker just copies last quarter's debt forward. It caught none of the thirty six new bonds. None. It still finds ninety point seven percent of all bonds, because most debt doesn't change in three months, and it gets eighteen of forty seven quarters exactly right. That is the number the agent has to beat.

shot.visual_intent: The zero is the hero and is drawn as an OUTLINED, LABELLED empty track — an absent bar reads as a rendering fault. The flattering numbers are deliberately smaller.

show.event: The track is drawn — and stays empty.
The two flattering numbers land beneath it, smaller.

props.sparkLine: A flattering number with a zero inside it.
props.title: What doing nothing misses
props.subtitle: The baseline: copy last quarter forward, over 47 dev quarters
props.trackLabel: New bonds caught by copying forward

stats.small: of all bonds it still finds — 87.5%–93.5%, because most debt simply carries over

props.whyNote: 90.7% is bond recall, and it is high for the same reason the zero is zero: a quarter's debt mostly does not move. The agent is not being asked to beat 90.7% — it is being asked to find what changed.
props.source: SOURCE: AI Debt Tracker docs/baseline_b0.md ← score_baseline.py dev · figdata.json

beats.narration_text: And the changes can be found. Of the thirty two new bonds that could be searched for, thirty were announced in a filing the agent could read in time. Of six early repayments, five were. So the distance between doing nothing and reading the filings is almost the whole gap. That is exactly what the agent has to win.

shot.visual_intent: ONE axis per claim, with the GAP drawn as a span. Two separate bars would show two quantities; the distance between them is the beat.

show.event: A span draws from 0 across to 30 on one axis.
The second axis draws the same distance on a smaller set.

props.subtitle: Each line runs from what copying forward catches to what was announced

props.searchNote: 32 of the 36 new bonds could be searched for at all — 4 carry no tagged interest rate. Of 16 bonds that disappeared, 9 simply reached their due date and 1 had no rate to search for, leaving 6.
props.source: SOURCE: AI Debt Tracker docs/changes_dev.md ← explain_changes.py · figdata.json

beats.narration_text: One surprise. E D G A R quietly moved forty three filing timestamps by four to five hours. The shift is four hours on summer dates and five in winter, which most likely means a time zone change. So the server that stops the agent seeing the future now anchors each cut off to the report itself, not to a clock.

shot.visual_intent: A cut-off that depends on a wall clock is a cut-off that can move without telling you. The drawing is the marker moving.

show.event: The count lands, then one filing's marker.
A dashed track draws the marker to its new position.

beats.narration_text: What this does not show. Ninety point seven percent is bond recall on forty seven dev quarters, with a range of eighty seven and a half to ninety three and a half. Ten of ten was calibrated on the same ten reports that found the bugs. And the agent itself still does not exist. Next: fix that company's data, check fresh reports, and build the document reader.

beats.narration_text: So: an answer key over one thousand and ninety three reports and nine thousand six hundred and fifty three bonds, and a grader that matches a bond on four fields and pairs each one only once. Checked against printed tables, it disagreed twice, and both times the grader was wrong, not the report. Ten of ten after five fixes is a calibration; two of three on untouched reports is the score. And doing nothing finds ninety one percent of bonds and none of the new ones.

shot.visual_intent: Judgment beat. The artifact page is the point (ILLUSTRATE LAW carve-out).

show.event: Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause.

props.artifactTitle: Building the Answer Key, Grader and Baseline
props.artifactHeading: What week 2 built, and what it is allowed to claim
artifactLines: An answer key over 1,093 reports from 100 companies — 9,653 bonds, Jan 2024 to Sep 2026. 900 of those reports list debt bond by bond; the rest give deals or totals, and are graded at the detail they give.

A bond counts as matched only if currency, interest rate, due year and amount (within 1%) all agree, and each true bond can be claimed by at most one answer. Every score carries a 95% bootstrap interval.

Against printed tables the grader agreed on 8 of 10 first pass. All 5 disagreements were bugs in the grader — repaid notes still counted, acquired debt dropped, two bonds in one entry, due dates read as issue dates, a currency never stated.
10 of 10 after the fixes is a CALIBRATION on the reports that found them. 2 of 3 on untouched reports is the measurement, and its one miss is the company's own tagging.
The do-nothing baseline finds 90.7% of bonds and 0 of 36 new ones, reproducing 18 of 47 quarters exactly. 30 of 32 new bonds were announced in time. That gap is the job.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Before you trust a score, check the thing that produced it against something printed by someone else. Mine was wrong in five ways, and every one of them would have quietly flattered whatever I built next.

shot.visual_intent: HANDOFF LAW: a real prompt, read ALOUD verbatim and then discussed. One of exactly two typing beats.
